Veterinary oxygen-carrier evidence.

Historical Oxyglobin regulatory evidence and the wider veterinary oxygen-carrier literature are presented together, with the population, endpoint and source boundaries kept explicit.

01FDA field trial02Evidence library03Regulatory records
Original FDA canine field trial

95% treatment success vs 32% control

FDA efficacy population: 20/21 Oxyglobin-treated dogs achieved treatment success versus 9/28 untreated controls; p≤0.001.

Intent-to-treat population: 73% (22/30) vs 29% (10/34); p≤0.001.

Treatment success meant no need for additional oxygen-carrying support for 24 hours. This was not a survival endpoint.

Pivotal multicenter field trial: 64 client-owned anaemic dogs; 30 randomized to Oxyglobin and 34 to untreated control.

Regulatory records

Oxyglobin is the historical veterinary HBOC precedent. The records below remain product-, species-, jurisdiction- and indication-specific.

FDA / EMA Oxyglobin source libraryOne regulatory route connecting the original US approval, EU authorisation and subsequent source documents.FDA original approval · NADA 141-067Primary FDA Freedom of Information summary. Approval date: 12 January 1998; indication: anaemia in dogs.EMA Oxyglobin EPAR · EMEA/V/C/000045Official European Medicines Agency record for Oxyglobin, haemoglobin glutamer-200 (bovine).

Evidence boundaries: the 95% vs 32% result is the FDA-defined 24-hour treatment-success endpoint in the Oxyglobin efficacy population, not survival. Historical Oxyglobin approvals do not establish BHOC efficacy, BHOC regulatory approval, approval for other species, affiliation or endorsement.

BHOC Veterinary Therapeutics, also known as BHOC Vet, is led by Archil Jaliashvili. The BHOC Species & Biodiversity Protection Initiative connects oxygen delivery science with the future of animal health and species protection.

Our foundation is comparative biology: different species have different blood group systems, yet most vertebrates share hemoglobin-based oxygen transport. We explore how this foundation can inform species-specific research and development.
